headline.main: Circumventing U.S. Sanctions: Turkish State-Owned Bank Suspected of Transferring $1.5 Billion to Tehran
headline.social: Circumventing U.S. Sanctions: Turkish State-Owned Bank Suspected of Transferring $1.5 Billion to Tehran

intro: For the last five years, prosecutors in the U.S. have been investigating the Turkish bank Halkbank of laundering billions of dollars on Iran’s behalf. Now, the bank is suspected of releasing sanctioned funds to Tehran.
text:
The Turkish state-owned bank Halkbank apparently assisted Iran to evade U.S. sanctions. DER SPIEGEL has learned that the financial institution is suspected of having released more than 1.5 billion euros out of a total volume of 4 billion euros for the regime in Tehran. According to sources in Western security circles, the money was allegedly transferred between May 2024 and March 2025, most of it in tranches of just under 200 million euros via shell companies.
Ever since the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel by the Palestinian terror organization Hamas, Tehran has been increasing its efforts to access billions in assets frozen around the world by sanctions. "This issue is our agenda and we continuously pursue it,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in January .
Because of the conflict with Israel, Iran’s military is facing a significant shortage of arms, as are the country’s allies in the region, such as the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israeli offensives have produced significant damage on the one hand, while, on the other, Tehran and the militias it supports have fired large numbers of missiles at Israel.
As a result, Tehran is in desperate need of hard currency to rebuild the stockpiles of its own military and those of Hezbollah, say international security experts. At the same time, Iran must fulfill obligations stemming from arms deals it signed with Russia.
Tehran scored a major success in its efforts to circumvent international sanctions at the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. According to international security experts, Iranian negotiators were able to score the release of crude oil stored in China worth almost $2 billion in an incident first reported by the Wall Street Journal .
Looking for Money from the Deutsche Börse
More recently, as DER SPIEGEL reported in March , Iran sought to access a portion of a sum, originally worth $4.9 million, that had been frozen by a Deutsche Börse subsidiary in Luxembourg.
In addition, emissaries from Tehran are thought to be trying to access $2.7 billion frozen in Malaysia to settle a lawsuit between the state-owned Iranian oil company and the Crescent Group from the United Arab Emirates.
That fact that the Turkish state-owned bank Halkbank is now suspected of helping Iran circumvent American sanctions is particularly sensitive: Prosecutors in New York have been investigating the Turkish financial institution since 2019 on suspicions of money laundering, fraud and conspiracy to commit a crime.
Faked Food Purchases
When that investigation began, U.S. prosecutors estimated that Halkbank had provided Tehran access to sanctioned funds totaling an estimated $20 billion. They claimed that oil revenues had been exchanged for gold to conceal money flows and that food purchases were faked using shell companies in Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
That case led to a diplomatic flareup between Ankara and Washington, with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan calling the case an "unlawful, ugly step.” A number of legal battles ensued.
Now, the spotlight is once again on Halkbank – as if the bank just carried on, business as usual. According to sources in Western security circles, the bank is suspected of having faked purchases of food and medicines through shell companies.
